title: The Fall of Tyre, Merchant of the Nations
summary: The last oracle against the nations is aimed at Tyre, the great Phoenician port whose ships and merchants dominated Mediterranean trade. Its harbor is ruined, the ships of Tarshish are told to wail, and Sidon is shamed, because the LORD of Hosts planned to humble the pride of the earth's renowned. After seventy years Tyre will be restored and trade again like a harlot hiring herself out, but in the end its profits will be set apart to the LORD for those who live before him.
story: The oracles began with Babylon, the great power of the east (chapter 13), and they end with Tyre, the great commercial power of the west. Between these two ends stands all the wealth and force of the known world, and all of it is placed under God's judgment. Babylon represents military empire; Tyre represents trade and wealth. Together they cover the two things nations most trust. Yet the collection closes, as Isaiah so often does, with a surprising turn toward hope: Tyre's wealth will finally serve the LORD. Chapters 24 to 27 then widen the view to the judgment and renewal of the whole earth.
historical:
Tyre, on the coast of what is now Lebanon, was the leading city of the Phoenicians, a Canaanite people famous for seafaring and trade. Its main city stood on an island just off the coast, making it very hard to besiege. Tyre's merchants traded throughout the Mediterranean and founded colonies, including Kition on Cyprus and Carthage in North Africa (traditionally founded in the late ninth century BC). Hiram of Tyre had supplied cedar and craftsmen for Solomon's temple (1 Kings 5). Sidon, a sister city to the north, was often linked with Tyre, and the two were sometimes ruled by the same king.

Tyre faced repeated attacks. In 701 BC Sennacherib's campaign drove Luli, king of Sidon, to flee by sea to Cyprus, as Sennacherib's own annals record, which fits verse 12's taunt that even in Cyprus there will be no rest. Later Assyrian kings, including Esarhaddon, also pressed Tyre. The Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar besieged Tyre for thirteen years in the early sixth century BC, according to the Jewish historian Josephus (compare Ezekiel 26 to 29), and in 332 BC Alexander the Great finally captured the island city by building a causeway out to it. Which of these events Isaiah's oracle first addressed is debated; many scholars favor the Assyrian period, while others see it fulfilled over this long series of blows. Verse 13, which points to the ruin of the land of the Chaldeans by the Assyrians, probably refers to Sennacherib's destruction of Babylon in 689 BC, offered as a warning: if Babylon could fall, so could Tyre. The Hebrew of that verse is difficult, and translations differ.
cultural:
Ships of Tarshish (verses 1, 6, 10, and 14) were large seagoing merchant ships, named for Tarshish, a distant port in the far west, perhaps Tartessos in southern Spain, though its location is uncertain. Such ships carried silver, tin, and other goods back to the eastern Mediterranean. Cyprus (Hebrew Kittim, after the city of Kition) was a key waystation. Tyre also grew rich by shipping Egyptian grain; Shihor was a name for a branch of the Nile, and verse 3 describes Egypt's harvest as Tyre's revenue. Tyre was famous for purple dye made from sea snails, a luxury good worn by royalty, and it is called the bestower of crowns because its wealth supported kings.

Verses 15 to 17 compare Tyre to a prostitute who has aged and been forgotten, walking the streets with a harp to attract customers again. The image is not mainly sexual. It describes commerce driven only by profit, selling to anyone for gain, a comparison also used for trade in Revelation 18. Seventy years, the span of a king's life, was a conventional figure for a full lifetime and appears in other ancient texts as a period of divine anger; Jeremiah uses it for Babylon's rule (Jeremiah 25:11-12).
literary: The oracle is framed by the cry, “Wail, O ships of Tarshish”, at verse 1 and verse 14, marking verses 1 to 14 as a complete lament. Inside the frame, the scene moves around the Mediterranean as the news spreads: Cyprus, Sidon, Egypt, Tarshish. At the center is a question and answer: “Who planned this against Tyre”? And the answer: “The LORD of Hosts planned it”. Verse 4 gives a striking personification: the sea itself speaks, saying it has borne no children, a lament over a city emptied of its young. Verses 15 to 18 are a prose postscript that looks beyond the fall to a restoration, ending on a note of holiness: Tyre's profits will be set apart to the LORD.

outline.t: Wail, ships of Tarshish: Tyre's harbor is ruined
Who planned this? The LORD of Hosts, to humble pride
God's hand over the sea and the lesson of the Chaldeans
Tyre forgotten seventy years, then restored, its profits set apart to the LORD

doctrines.note: The question of verse 8 has one answer: the LORD of Hosts planned it. Even the world's markets and trade routes are subject to God's purposes, and he stretches out his hand over the sea.
Tyre's sin is pride in its wealth and a commerce that sells itself to anyone for gain. The chapter judges not trade itself but trade that becomes an idol and a source of arrogance.
The final verse says Tyre's profits will be holy to the LORD, set apart for his purposes and his people. What was used for pride can be consecrated to God.
The chapter ends with the wealth of the nations flowing to those who live before the LORD. Isaiah later develops this into a vision of the nations bringing their wealth to Zion (Isaiah 60).

words.note: Tsor, Tyre, meaning rock, after the rocky island on which the city stood. The name appears six times in the chapter. Tyre's rocky island made it seem invulnerable, but the chapter shows that even the rock cannot stand against the LORD's plan.

Sachar, profit or merchandise, gain from trade. It appears three times, describing Tyre's revenue from Egypt's grain and its wealth from trade. Verse 18 says this profit will finally be set apart to the LORD rather than hoarded.

Etnan, the wages or hire of a prostitute. Deuteronomy 23:18 forbids bringing such wages into the house of the LORD, which makes verse 18 all the more surprising: Tyre's hire becomes holy to God. The image shows God redeeming what was corrupt rather than merely condemning it.

Qodesh, holiness or something set apart. In verse 18 Tyre's profits and wages become qodesh to the LORD. The word marks the final transformation of the chapter, from a city of pride to a source of provision for God's people.

christ: Jesus's ministry reached the region of Tyre and Sidon, where he healed the daughter of a Syrophoenician woman who asked for the crumbs from the children's table (Mark 7:24-30). He said that if his miracles had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago (Matthew 11:21-22), turning this old symbol of pride into a judgment on his own unrepentant hearers. By the time of Paul, there were disciples in Tyre who welcomed him and prayed with him on the beach (Acts 21:3-6), a small fulfillment of the chapter's hope that Tyre would one day belong to the LORD. Revelation 18, in its lament over Babylon's fall, draws on this chapter and on Ezekiel's oracles against Tyre, showing that the fall of proud commerce is part of the story Christ completes.

hard.q: What are the seventy years of verse 15, and did the prophecy come true?
hard.a: Interpreters take the seventy years in two main ways. Some read them as a specific period and propose historical spans: from the Assyrian subjugation of Tyre around 700 BC to the weakening of Assyria about seventy years later, or from Nebuchadnezzar's pressure on Tyre to the restoration of trade under Persian rule. Others read seventy years as a round number for a full lifetime, the span of a king's life, as the text itself says, meaning that Tyre would be humbled for a generation and then recover. Both readings agree that Tyre did recover and continued as a trading city for centuries, and that it contributed to the building of the Second Temple (Ezra 3:7 mentions cedar supplied by the people of Tyre and Sidon). Readers also differ on verse 18: some see it fulfilled in such contributions, others in the later spread of the gospel to Tyre, and others in a future gathering of the nations' wealth to God.

questions: Tyre was a city built on trade and wealth. How does this chapter challenge the way you think about money and success?
The chapter asks, who planned this? When disaster strikes the powerful, how does trust in God's sovereignty shape your response?
Tyre's profits end up set apart to the LORD. What would it look like for your own resources to be holy to the LORD?
